clips.syllabus: Von Neumann architecture, fetch-decode-execute cycle
clips.title: Von Neumann Model: Stored Program and Sequential Processing
clips.hook: Unified memory, bit interpretation by access stage, and PC-driven sequential execution.
clips.summary: The two defining properties are the stored-program concept (unified linear memory where bits are interpreted as instruction or data based on the stage accessing them) and sequential instruction processing governed by the PC. The PC advances by instruction size except for control-transfer instructions, which implement loops and conditionals.
clips.videoTitle: Digital Design & Computer Architecture - Lecture 11: Microarchitecture I (ETH Zürich, Spring 2020)

quiz.question: In a von Neumann machine, how does the hardware decide whether a memory word is an instruction or data?
options: By the opcode field of the word itself always
By the stage of processing accessing it (fetch vs. data access)
A tag bit stored with every word
By the memory region's separate physical bank
quiz.explanation: Memory is unified and untyped; interpretation depends on whether it is accessed in instruction fetch or operand fetch.

clips.syllabus: Von Neumann architecture, fetch-decode-execute cycle
clips.title: Dataflow vs Von Neumann: No PC, Token-Driven Firing
clips.hook: What if instructions fire when operands are ready, with no program counter?
clips.summary: In the dataflow model there is no program counter; an instruction is fetched and executed when all its input operands (tokens) are available, and each instruction names its consumers. This exposes much more parallelism than the von Neumann model's sequential ordering.
clips.videoTitle: Digital Design & Computer Architecture - Lecture 11: Microarchitecture I (ETH Zürich, Spring 2020)

quiz.question: What determines when an instruction executes in a pure dataflow machine?
options: A compiler-inserted schedule slot
The program counter reaching it
Clock cycle count modulo pipeline depth
Availability of all its input operand tokens
quiz.explanation: Firing is triggered by operand availability; there is no PC.

clips.syllabus: Von Neumann architecture, fetch-decode-execute cycle
clips.title: Why Multi-Cycle Beats Single-Cycle: Slowest Stage vs Slowest Instruction
clips.hook: Split instruction processing into stages so the cycle time follows the slowest stage.
clips.summary: The six phases of the instruction cycle all fit in one cycle in a single-cycle machine, whereas multi-cycle machines can spend several cycles per phase. The cycle time is set by the slowest stage rather than the slowest instruction, though both still follow sequential von Neumann semantics.
clips.videoTitle: Digital Design & Computer Architecture - Lecture 11: Microarchitecture I (ETH Zürich, Spring 2020)

clips.syllabus: Von Neumann architecture, fetch-decode-execute cycle
clips.title: Iron Law of Performance: Single vs Multi-Cycle
clips.hook: Time = instructions × CPI × cycle time, applied to microarchitecture choices.
clips.summary: Execution time is instruction count times average CPI times cycle time. Single-cycle has CPI=1 but a long cycle; multi-cycle gets short cycles and a low average CPI by weighting frequent cheap instructions, giving two independent optimization knobs.
clips.videoTitle: Digital Design & Computer Architecture - Lecture 11: Microarchitecture I (ETH Zürich, Spring 2020)

quiz.question: A single-cycle machine has which iron-law property?
options: CPI above 1
CPI of 1 with a long cycle time
CPI varies, short cycle
Fewer instructions
quiz.explanation: Every instruction takes one cycle, but the cycle must fit the longest instruction.

clips.syllabus: Bayes' rule, base rates; common distributions
clips.title: Accurate test, low PPV: sensitivity, specificity, base rate
clips.hook: Why a test with 90% sensitivity and 91% specificity gives only ~1/11 chance of disease given positive.
clips.concept: Positive predictive value and base rate
clips.summary: With 1% prevalence, 9 true positives and 89 false positives give PPV = 9/98 ≈ 1/11. Test accuracy is two numbers (sensitivity, specificity) and neither alone gives P(disease | positive); the base rate dominates.
clips.videoTitle: The medical test paradox, and redesigning Bayes' rule

quiz.question: In a population with 1% prevalence, a test has 90% sensitivity and ~9% false positive rate. Why is P(disease | positive) only about 1/11?
options: Specificity and sensitivity cancel each other
Sensitivity is too low to detect disease
False positives from the large healthy group (~89) greatly outnumber true positives (~9)
The test is biased toward healthy patients
quiz.explanation: Because the healthy group is 99x larger, even a 9% false positive rate yields about 89 false positives versus 9 true positives, so PPV = 9/98.

clips.syllabus: Bayes' rule, base rates; common distributions
clips.title: Bayes factor: tests update priors, not give answers
clips.hook: Reduce sensitivity and FPR to a single likelihood ratio and use it to approximate posteriors.
clips.summary: A test updates a prior; the relevant number for a positive result is the Bayes factor = sensitivity / false positive rate (here 10). For small priors, multiplying by it approximates the posterior, but it fails for large priors (10% gives 53%, not 100%).
clips.videoTitle: The medical test paradox, and redesigning Bayes' rule

quiz.question: Why does the rule 'posterior ≈ prior × Bayes factor' fail for a 10% prior with Bayes factor 10?
options: The false positive rate becomes zero
Bayes factor changes with the prior
Sensitivity must be recomputed
It treats probabilities as if they were unbounded; it only holds approximately when the prior is small
quiz.explanation: Multiplication is exact for odds, not probabilities. For small probabilities odds ≈ probability, but at 10% it overshoots (true answer 9/17 ≈ 53%).

clips.syllabus: Bayes' rule, base rates; common distributions
clips.title: Bayes' rule in odds form: posterior odds = prior odds × BF
clips.hook: Why Bayesian updating is exactly multiplication once you switch from probabilities to odds.
clips.summary: Odds are positives to negatives; filtering to positive results scales the diseased count by sensitivity and the healthy count by FPR, so posterior odds = prior odds × Bayes factor exactly. Examples: 1:99 → 10:99 (~1/11), 1:9 → 10:9 (53%), BF 90 gives ~48%.
clips.videoTitle: The medical test paradox, and redesigning Bayes' rule

quiz.question: Prior probability is 10% (odds 1:9) and the Bayes factor is 10. What is the posterior probability?
quiz.explanation: Posterior odds = 1:9 × 10 = 10:9, so probability = 10/19 ≈ 53%.

clips.syllabus: Process vs thread, PCB, context switch
clips.title: Dispatcher context switch and dispatch latency
clips.hook: Step by step: what the dispatcher saves and restores, and why its latency is pure overhead.
clips.summary: The dispatcher saves the running process's CPU state into its PCB, picks the next PCB from the ready queue, restores its registers and PC, and switches to user mode. This takes CPU time (dispatch latency), so it must be extremely fast; the scheduler decides, the dispatcher executes.
clips.videoTitle: The Fancy Algorithms That Make Your Computer Feel Smoother

quiz.question: What is the division of responsibility between scheduler and dispatcher?
options: Scheduler performs context switch, dispatcher picks the process
Dispatcher manages I/O queues, scheduler manages ready queue
Both pick processes, differing only in queue type
Scheduler picks the next process per policy, dispatcher performs the context switch
quiz.explanation: The scheduler applies the policy to the ready queue; the dispatcher saves/restores state and hands over the CPU.

clips.syllabus: CPU scheduling: FCFS, SJF, RR, priority, MLFQ
clips.title: FCFS and the convoy effect
clips.hook: How one CPU-bound process starves I/O-bound ones and idles both CPU and devices.
clips.summary: With FCFS, a CPU-bound process holds the CPU while I/O-bound processes finish I/O and pile up in the ready queue, leaving devices idle. Then the CPU idles when they run briefly, lowering CPU and device utilization.
clips.videoTitle: The Fancy Algorithms That Make Your Computer Feel Smoother

quiz.question: What causes the convoy effect under FCFS?
options: Short I/O-bound processes waiting behind a long CPU burst, leaving I/O devices idle
Time quantum too small
Priority inversion
Too many context switches
quiz.explanation: Short bursts queue behind a long one, so device and CPU utilization alternate in idle phases.

clips.syllabus: CPU scheduling: FCFS, SJF, RR, priority, MLFQ
clips.title: Why SJF minimizes average waiting time
clips.hook: The exchange argument: moving a short job ahead helps more than it hurts.
clips.summary: SJF picks the shortest next CPU burst using a priority queue, with FCFS tie-breaking. Moving a short process before a long one reduces the short one's wait more than it increases the long one's, so average waiting time is minimized.
clips.videoTitle: The Fancy Algorithms That Make Your Computer Feel Smoother

quiz.question: Why is SJF optimal for average waiting time?
options: It minimizes context switches
It gives equal CPU shares
It uses preemption
Swapping a shorter job ahead decreases its wait by more than it increases the longer job's wait
quiz.explanation: Each swap of an out-of-order pair reduces the sum of waiting times.

clips.syllabus: CPU scheduling: FCFS, SJF, RR, priority, MLFQ
clips.title: Predicting CPU bursts with exponential averaging
clips.hook: τ(n+1)=α·t(n)+(1−α)·τ(n): why one number of state suffices.
clips.summary: Since the next burst is unknowable, SJF estimates it by exponential averaging of past bursts. Expanding the recursion shows older bursts are weighted by α(1−α)^k, decaying exponentially, and only the last prediction needs storing; α=0 ignores recent, α=1 ignores history.
clips.videoTitle: The Fancy Algorithms That Make Your Computer Feel Smoother

quiz.question: In τ(n+1)=α·t(n)+(1−α)·τ(n), what happens when α=1?
options: Prediction ignores the latest burst
Prediction equals only the most recent actual burst
Prediction stays constant at the initial value
Prediction is the average of all bursts
quiz.explanation: With α=1 the (1−α) term vanishes, so τ(n+1)=t(n).

clips.syllabus: CPU scheduling: FCFS, SJF, RR, priority, MLFQ
clips.title: Preemptive vs non-preemptive scheduling and starvation
clips.hook: Why non-preemptive scheduling is dangerous and how SJF can starve long jobs.
clips.summary: Non-preemptive schedulers rely on processes yielding, so an infinite loop without syscalls can freeze the system. Starvation is a policy property: in SJF, long-burst processes can wait indefinitely while shorter ones keep arriving.
clips.videoTitle: The Fancy Algorithms That Make Your Computer Feel Smoother

quiz.question: Why can SJF starve a process?
options: A long-burst process may never be chosen while shorter bursts keep arriving
It has no priority concept
Its context switches are too costly
It uses a FIFO queue
quiz.explanation: Starvation arises from the policy ordering by burst length.

clips.syllabus: CPU scheduling: FCFS, SJF, RR, priority, MLFQ
clips.title: Round Robin and the time quantum trade-off
clips.hook: Timer interrupts, the (n−1)q wait bound, and why quantum size matters.
clips.summary: RR uses a FIFO ready queue plus a hardware timer interrupt after one quantum. With n processes each waits at most (n−1)q; a huge quantum degenerates to FCFS, while a tiny one wastes time in context switches.
clips.videoTitle: The Fancy Algorithms That Make Your Computer Feel Smoother

quiz.question: What happens in RR if the quantum is much larger than typical CPU bursts?
options: Context switches rise sharply
Starvation occurs
It behaves like FCFS
It becomes SJF
quiz.explanation: Processes block for I/O before the timer fires, so no preemption occurs.

clips.syllabus: CPU scheduling: FCFS, SJF, RR, priority, MLFQ
clips.title: Priority scheduling, starvation and aging
clips.hook: Priority queues, SJF as a special case, and aging to avoid indefinite blocking.
clips.summary: Priority scheduling uses integer priorities and can combine with RR within a level. Low-priority processes may starve, as in SJF, which is priority by inverse predicted burst; aging gradually raises waiting processes' priority to guarantee eventual execution.
clips.videoTitle: The Fancy Algorithms That Make Your Computer Feel Smoother

quiz.question: How does aging prevent starvation?
options: Uses FCFS
Gradually raises priority of waiting processes
Increases time quantum over time
Kills high-priority processes
quiz.explanation: Eventually a waiting process reaches the highest priority.

clips.syllabus: CPU scheduling: FCFS, SJF, RR, priority, MLFQ
clips.title: Multilevel feedback queue mechanics
clips.hook: How MLFQ demotes CPU-bound processes and keeps interactive ones high.
clips.summary: In MLFQ processes start in the top queue; using a whole quantum demotes them to lower queues with larger quanta, while processes finishing bursts early stay or move up. Behavior thus automatically sorts I/O-bound from CPU-bound processes.
clips.videoTitle: The Fancy Algorithms That Make Your Computer Feel Smoother

quiz.question: In MLFQ, what causes a process to be demoted?
options: Waiting long in ready queue
Using its entire time quantum without finishing its CPU burst
Having a short burst
Making an I/O request
quiz.explanation: Exceeding the quantum signals CPU-bound behavior.

clips.syllabus: Keys: primary, candidate, foreign, super
clips.title: Candidate keys: uniqueness across time, not just now
clips.hook: Why a column that is currently unique, like state capital, is still not a candidate key.
clips.summary: A candidate key is a minimal unique identifier, and the primary key is chosen from the candidates. An attribute that is unique only by accident of current data, such as state capital, does not qualify. It must be guaranteed unique for all possible future data.
clips.videoTitle: Database Keys Made Easy - Primary, Foreign, Candidate, Surrogate, & Many More

quiz.question: A table's current rows all have distinct values in column X. When is X a candidate key?
options: Always, since it is unique
Only if uniqueness is guaranteed by the domain semantics for all possible future rows
Only if X is an integer
Only if X is not the primary key
quiz.explanation: Keys are constraints on all legal instances, not properties of the current instance.

clips.syllabus: Keys: primary, candidate, foreign, super
clips.title: Super keys and irreducibility
clips.hook: Why (state_code, region) is a super key but not a candidate key.
clips.summary: A candidate key is an irreducible set of attributes that guarantees uniqueness, meaning no attribute can be removed. A super key is any superset of a candidate key. Using a super key as the primary key allows semantically duplicate rows, such as two Georgias.
clips.videoTitle: Database Keys Made Easy - Primary, Foreign, Candidate, Surrogate, & Many More

quiz.question: Which statement about super keys is correct?
options: Every super key is a candidate key
A super key contains a candidate key and may have extra attributes
A super key can contain NULLs but a candidate key cannot
A super key must be a single attribute
quiz.explanation: A candidate key is a minimal super key. Super keys can be supersets of candidate keys.

clips.syllabus: Keys: primary, candidate, foreign, super
clips.title: Surrogate vs natural keys: choosing a primary key
clips.hook: A surrogate key alone doesn't prevent duplicate entities. Use alternate keys, and know when ISBN fails.
clips.summary: A surrogate key without an alternate key on the natural attribute lets duplicate real-world entities exist under different IDs. Natural keys like ISBN may not cover all rows, such as ebooks, so an invented key is a better primary key.
clips.videoTitle: Database Keys Made Easy - Primary, Foreign, Candidate, Surrogate, & Many More

quiz.question: Why add an alternate (unique) key on state_code when state_id is a surrogate primary key?
options: To prevent two different state_ids from representing the same real state
To allow NULL state_ids
To make state_id composite
To speed up joins on state_id
quiz.explanation: A surrogate key only guarantees row distinctness, so uniqueness of the natural candidate key must be enforced separately.

clips.syllabus: ISA: RISC vs CISC (MIPS vs x86)
clips.title: RISC Philosophy: Simple ISA, Smart Compiler, Dumb Hardware
clips.hook: Why early RISC kept instructions minimal and pushed scheduling and dependency handling into the compiler.
clips.summary: RISC (IBM 801, then MIPS and SPARC) favored very simple instructions, with no string copy and initially no multiply or byte loads. Hardware does little decoding, no dependency checking and no reordering, so it can clock faster and be easier to design. The compiler carries the complexity: it translates to simple instructions and reorders them for performance.
clips.videoTitle: Digital Design & Computer Architecture - Lecture 19a: VLIW (ETH Zürich, Spring 2021)

quiz.question: Which choice best reflects the original RISC design philosophy as described here?
options: Simple instructions with minimal decode, with the compiler reordering code and hardware doing little dependency checking
Complex instructions such as string copy, so the hardware can do more work per instruction
Compiling programs directly to a variable-length microcode format
Hardware dynamic reordering of instructions to hide compiler inefficiencies
quiz.explanation: RISC keeps hardware simple (little decoding, no dependency checking or reordering) to enable higher frequency and easier design. The compiler does the scheduling and the hard work.

clips.syllabus: Expectation, variance, covariance; CLT; hypothesis tests and p-values
clips.title: Variance Adds, Standard Deviation Scales as √n
clips.hook: Why sums of n i.i.d. variables have mean nμ and standard deviation σ√n.
clips.summary: Variance is E[(X-μ)²]; for independent variables variances add, not standard deviations. So a sum of n copies has mean nμ and std σ√n, so spread grows slowly, and rescaling to mean 0 and std 1 reveals a universal shape.
clips.videoTitle: But what is the Central Limit Theorem?

quiz.question: X has standard deviation σ. For the sum of n independent copies of X, what is the standard deviation?
options: nσ
σ/√n
σ
σ√n
quiz.explanation: Variances of independent variables add, giving nσ², so the std is σ√n.

clips.syllabus: Expectation, variance, covariance; CLT; hypothesis tests and p-values
clips.title: Formal CLT: Standardized Sums Converge to N(0,1)
clips.hook: The rigorous statement: the z-score of a sum has probabilities converging to the standard normal integral.
clips.summary: Subtract the mean nμ and divide by σ√n to measure the sum in standard deviations. The CLT states that P(a ≤ Z_n ≤ b) converges to the area under the standard normal density between a and b as n→∞, regardless of the original distribution.
clips.videoTitle: But what is the Central Limit Theorem?

quiz.question: What does the standardized quantity (S_n − nμ)/(σ√n) converge to in distribution?
options: The standard normal N(0,1)
A uniform distribution
The original distribution of X
A normal with mean nμ
quiz.explanation: It has mean 0 and std 1 and converges to N(0,1) by CLT.

clips.syllabus: Expectation, variance, covariance; CLT; hypothesis tests and p-values
clips.title: CLT in Practice: 95% Interval for 100 Die Rolls
clips.hook: Use mean, variance and the 68-95-99.7 rule to bound a sum, and see how sample means concentrate.
clips.summary: For a fair die μ=3.5 and σ≈1.71, so the sum of 100 rolls is approximately N(350, 17.1²). A 95% range is about ±2σ, i.e. 316 to 384; dividing by 100 gives the range of the sample mean.
clips.videoTitle: But what is the Central Limit Theorem?

quiz.question: A sum of 100 fair die rolls has mean 350 and std 17.1. Which interval gives roughly 95% coverage?
quiz.explanation: About 95% lies within two standard deviations: 350 ± 34.2.

clips.syllabus: Expectation, variance, covariance; CLT; hypothesis tests and p-values
clips.title: When the CLT Fails: i.i.d. and Finite Variance Assumptions
clips.hook: Independence, identical distribution and finite variance: what breaks without each.
clips.summary: The classical CLT needs independent, identically distributed terms with finite variance. Dependence or non-identical distributions need generalizations, and heavy-tailed distributions with infinite variance may converge to a non-normal limit.
clips.videoTitle: But what is the Central Limit Theorem?

quiz.question: Which situation can cause sums of i.i.d. variables to NOT approach a normal distribution?
options: The variable has infinite variance
The sum has fewer than 1000 terms
The variable is skewed
The variable is discrete
quiz.explanation: Classical CLT requires finite variance; heavy-tailed laws can converge to non-Gaussian stable distributions.
